newsitem.title: FRANCE: Changes ahead among French, not UK, left-wingers.
newsitem.headline: Changes ahead among French, not UK, left-wingers.

text.p: The European Parliament on Friday named the French Socialists who will replace the four Euro-MPs leaving the EU assembly to serve in the government of new French Socialist prime minister Lionel Jospin.
Georges Garot, Marie-Noel Lienemann, Olivier Duhamel and Jean-Louis Cottigny will replace Elisabeth Guigou, Catherine Trautmann, Bernard Kouchner and Pierre Moscovici.

Replacements for three other French Socialists who are leaving the European Parliament to take their seats in the French National Assembly -- Nicole Pery, Jack Lang and Frederique Breding -- have not yet been confirmed.

Elisabeth Guigou, 50, who has been appointed French justice minister, has won plaudits as one of two European Parliament representatives to European government negotiations on the reform of the Maastricht treaty.
A skilled technocrat, she was catapulted to prominence as France's European affairs minister during negotiations on the original Maastricht Treaty.
Strasbourg's Socialist mayor Catherine Trautmann, 46, becomes minister of culture and communications, and government spokeswoman.

She is better known for her efforts as mayor to improve the city where the European Parliament has its seat and for leading a dogged resistance to the far right than for her presence in the assembly itself.
Trautmann had Strasbourg's statue of Joan of Arc removed to prevent the Front from staging a ceremony around it in April.
Her relations with Jospin are cool owing to her loyalty to former Socialist prime minister Michel Rocard, who now chairs the European Parliament's development committee.
Bernard Kouchner, 57, is the new secretary of state (junior minister) for health.
The founder of the Medecins sans Frontieres medical charity has stirred both admiration as the champion of refugees and war victims, and antipathy for his publicity-seeking.
As France's minister for humanitarian action in 1991-93, he persuaded the United Nations to back the right to humanitarian intervention in civil wars.
He was less well appreciated as chairman of the European Parliament's development committee from 1994 to 1996.

A former member of the French and European Socialist parties, he switched to the centre-left French Radical party in January 1996 and joined its European counterpart, the European Radical Alliance a year later.

French Socialist Party secretary Pierre Moscovici, who has kept a low profile in the European Parliament, will hold the European affairs portfolio, serving as minister delegate to foreign minister Hubert Vedrine.
Meanwhile, the European Parliamentary Labour Party has voted to keep its current leader, Wayne David, who has led the EPLP since 1994.
David fought off a leadership challenge from Alan Donnelly, a prominent member of the parliament's economic and monetary affairs committee.
The challenge came six months before Britain's new Labour government takes over the presidency of the EU.
In a statement issued on Wednesday the EPLP said it expected its leader to play a key role during Britain's EU presidency from January to June 1998.

"During that time the British Government will look to their Labour colleagues in the European Parliament to provide maximum support for those British proposals which require the endorsement of the parliament," the statement said.
